title: Vision-language-action models: RT-2, OpenVLA and pi0
summary: How a vision-language model becomes a robot policy: actions as 256-bin tokens (RT-2, OpenVLA), compressed DCT tokens (FAST), and flow-matching action chunks (pi0).
outcomes: Explain how RT-2 and OpenVLA turn a continuous action into one discrete token per dimension and back
Compute bin indices, token ids and the worst-case quantization error of a binned action
Explain why per-step tokens struggle at high control rates and how FAST's DCT plus BPE fixes it
Trace pi0's flow-matching action expert as it denoises an action chunk with Euler steps
Choose between per-step control, chunk execution and temporal ensembling for a given robot

lessons.title: From a VLM that describes to a VLA that acts

blocks.md: A **robot policy** maps an observation (camera images, often the robot's joint angles) and a task instruction to an **action**: the command sent to the robot's controller at each control step. Policies trained from scratch on robot demonstrations only know what those demonstrations show. Demonstrations are slow and expensive to collect, so such policies tend to break on new objects, new backgrounds and new phrasings of the instruction.

A **vision-language model** (VLM) already handles new objects and phrasings, because it was trained on web-scale image and text data. Recall the recipe: a vision encoder turns the image into patch embeddings, a projector maps them into the language model's embedding space, and the LLM reads them like words. RT-2 (Brohan et al., 2023) asked: what if the answer the VLM writes is the robot's next move? The authors called the result a **vision-language-action model** (VLA).

RT-2 fine-tunes PaLI-X (5B and 55B) and PaLM-E (12B) on robot data phrased as visual question answering: the prompt is "Q: what action should the robot take to [task instruction]? A:" and the target answer is a string of action tokens. A key detail is **co-fine-tuning**: robot data is mixed with the original web data in each batch instead of fine-tuning on robot data alone, which the authors found generalizes better.

What is an action? RT-2's action is a 6-DoF displacement of the **end-effector** (the gripper at the tip of the arm): $\Delta x, \Delta y, \Delta z$ and three rotation deltas, plus gripper extension and a terminate flag. Open X-Embodiment and OpenVLA use the same idea as a **7-DoF** vector: 3 position, 3 rotation, 1 gripper. "DoF" means degrees of freedom, one number per controllable quantity.

blocks.title: OpenVLA: image and instruction in, 7 action tokens out

scenes.caption: The image passes through two pretrained vision encoders. Prismatic, the VLM OpenVLA starts from, concatenates DINOv2 features (spatial detail) and SigLIP features (semantics) for each patch.
A small 2-layer MLP projects the fused patch features into Llama 2's embedding space, where they sit next to the tokenized instruction.
The LLM decodes 7 tokens one after another with its ordinary next-token head. Nothing in the architecture is new: actions are just words from a reserved part of the vocabulary.
A de-tokenizer maps each token back to a continuous value and the robot executes it. OpenVLA reports about 6 Hz on one RTX 4090 in bfloat16 without inference speedups.

blocks.md: A VLA is a VLM whose output vocabulary also contains actions. Predicting the robot's next move becomes one more question the model answers, so the whole web-pretrained network is reused for control.

Where does robot data come from? The **Open X-Embodiment** dataset pooled 60 existing datasets from 34 labs into one format (RLDS): more than 1M real robot trajectories across 22 embodiments. Actions are only **coarsely aligned**: each dataset is converted to a 7-DoF end-effector action and normalized separately, but coordinate frames are not aligned and values may be absolute or relative positions or velocities. OpenVLA curated 970k episodes from it (single-arm, end-effector control, at least one third-person camera).

Does it work? OpenVLA (7B) beats the closed RT-2-X (55B) by 16.5% absolute task success across 29 evaluation tasks, with 7x fewer parameters. RT-2's authors are careful about what web data buys: generalization to novel objects and semantically varied instructions, while "the model's physical skills are still limited to the distribution of skills seen in the robot data".
Misconception: web pretraining teaches the robot new motions. It does not. Web knowledge helps decide *which* object and *where*; the motor skills themselves still come from robot demonstrations.

blocks.question: In Open X-Embodiment, two robots receive the identical 7-number action vector. Why might they move very differently?
options: The 256-bin tokenizer uses a different vocabulary for each robot
Actions are normalized per dataset and frames and control modes (position vs velocity, absolute vs relative) are not aligned, so the same numbers mean different motions
Open X-Embodiment stores only images, so actions are re-estimated per robot
The model adds a robot-specific noise term at inference
blocks.explain: The paper says the alignment is coarse: each dataset's actions are normalized separately and coordinate frames are not aligned, so an output is de-normalized differently per embodiment and the same vector can induce very different motions.

blocks.question: During a robot task, RT-2 restricts decoding to valid action tokens only. What failure does this prevent?
options: The model running out of GPU memory
Cross-entropy loss becoming negative
The model answering with ordinary words that cannot be turned into a robot command
Image tokens being emitted as output
blocks.explain: RT-2 must output something executable. Constraining the output vocabulary to the 256 action tokens on robot prompts guarantees a parsable action, while the same model still answers normal vision-language questions with full text.

lessons.title: Binning: one 7-DoF action becomes seven tokens

blocks.md: An LLM can only emit tokens from a finite vocabulary, but robot actions are continuous. RT-2's answer, reused by OpenVLA, is **uniform binning**: each action dimension is discretized separately into one of **256 bins** of equal width between a lower bound $lo$ and an upper bound $hi$. A 7-DoF action becomes 7 integers in 0 to 255, and each integer is mapped to one token.

blocks.tex: w = \frac{hi - lo}{256},\qquad b = \operatorname{clip}\!\left(\left\lfloor \frac{a - lo}{w} \right\rfloor, 0, 255\right),\qquad \hat a = lo + \left(b + \tfrac12\right) w
blocks.caption: Encode a value a to bin b, decode b to the bin center. The error is at most half a bin: |a minus decoded a| is at most w/2 for values inside the bounds.

blocks.md: Which tokens? PaLI-X has a token for every integer up to 1000, so RT-2 simply writes numbers, like "1 128 91 241 5 101 127". PaLM-E and Llama have no such tokens, so RT-2-PaLM-E and OpenVLA **overwrite the 256 least-used tokens**. In the Llama tokenizer those are the last 256 ids. With a 32,000-token vocabulary, OpenVLA's code maps bin $b$ to token id $31999 - b$, so ids 31744 to 31999 now mean actions.

Toy bounds for our example: positions $\Delta x, \Delta y, \Delta z$ in [-0.05, 0.05] m, rotations in [-0.25, 0.25] rad, gripper in [0, 1]. So $w$ is 0.000391 m for positions, 0.00195 rad for rotations and 0.0039 for the gripper. The action is $a = (0.012, -0.031, 0.004, 0.10, -0.02, 0.18, 1.0)$.

blocks.prompt: The gripper value is exactly 1.0, the upper bound. The formula gives floor((1.0 - 0)/0.0039) = 256. What happens, and what comes back after decoding?
blocks.reveal: Bin 256 does not exist, so the clip puts it in bin 255, the top bin. Decoding returns its center, $0 + 255.5 / 256 = 0.998$, an error of 0.00195: exactly half a bin. Values at or beyond the bounds always land in an edge bin.

scenes.caption: Columns in order: dx, dy, dz, droll, dpitch, dyaw, gripper. Positions are in meters, rotations in radians, the gripper is 0 (closed) to 1 (open). Each dimension is binned independently.
Bin each value. dx: (0.012 + 0.05) / 0.000391 = 158.7, floor 158. The gripper's 256 is clipped to 255.
Map each bin to a reserved token, id = 31999 - b. The LLM is trained to emit exactly these 7 ids, one per decode step.
Decode: token to bin to bin center. The robot receives these values, not the originals.
Quantization error (times 1000). Positions are off by at most 0.195 mm, rotations by at most 0.98 mrad, the gripper by 1.95 thousandths: each is within half a bin.

blocks.md: Simplified: OpenVLA's released code first normalizes each dimension to [-1, 1] and places 256 evenly spaced bin *edges* (255 intervals), folding the top index into the last interval. The idea and the error bound are the same; the exact centers differ slightly.

How should $lo$ and $hi$ be chosen? RT-2 used the min and max of the data. OpenVLA instead uses the **1st and 99th percentiles** of each dimension, because a single outlier can stretch the interval and waste most bins. In a synthetic $\Delta x$ dataset (10,000 values, mostly within plus or minus 0.06 m) plus one outlier at 0.5 m, the middle 98% of the data lands in only 40 of the 256 bins under min-max bounds.

blocks.title: Bin width for dx under different bounds

scenes.caption: Clean synthetic data spans [-0.06, 0.06] m, so a bin is 0.12 m / 256 = 0.47 mm wide.
One bad demonstration at 0.5 m stretches the min-max interval to 0.56 m: bins become 2.19 mm wide, almost 5 times coarser for every normal action.
Percentile bounds ignore the outlier: [-0.043, 0.042] m gives 0.33 mm bins. Values outside are clipped to the edge bins, which is rare by construction.

blocks.md: Training is plain next-token prediction with cross-entropy computed on the action tokens only. OpenVLA's findings: fine-tune the vision encoder too (freezing it hurt), and train for many epochs (27, until action-token accuracy passed 95%), unlike typical 1 to 2 epoch LLM runs. The full run took 64 A100s for 14 days.

To adapt to a new robot, OpenVLA's **LoRA** (low-rank adapters on all linear layers) fine-tuning at rank 32 reached 68.2% success versus 69.7% for full fine-tuning, while training only 1.4% of the parameters, on a single A100 in 10 to 15 hours.

blocks.question: A dimension has bounds [-0.05, 0.05] m and 256 uniform bins. For an action inside the bounds, what is the largest possible decoding error?
options: 0.39 mm, one full bin
0.195 mm, half a bin
0.05 m, half the range
Zero, because the token stores the exact value
blocks.explain: The bin width is 0.1 m / 256 = 0.39 mm. Decoding returns the bin center, so the worst case is a value at a bin edge: half a bin, 0.195 mm.

blocks.question: Your dataset has a few teleoperation glitches with huge rotation values. Training with min-max bounds, the robot's wrist motions become jerky and imprecise. What is the most likely cause?
options: The glitches widened the interval, so normal rotations share very few, very wide bins
The LLM's vocabulary is too small to hold 256 tokens
Cross-entropy cannot be used for rotation dimensions
Binning rotations requires 512 bins by definition
blocks.explain: Outliers set the min and max, so the bin width grows and most real actions collapse into a handful of bins. This is exactly why OpenVLA bins between the 1st and 99th percentiles.

lessons.title: Why per-step tokens break at 50 Hz, and how FAST compresses them

blocks.md: The **control frequency** is how many actions per second the robot's controller expects. Datasets in the FAST paper range from 5 Hz (BridgeData V2) and 15 Hz (DROID) to 50 Hz (bimanual shirt folding); ALOHA, the hardware ACT was built on, records at 50 Hz. Per-step binning emits one token per action dimension per step, so the token rate grows linearly with frequency: $D \times f$ tokens per second for $D$ dimensions.

blocks.title: Action tokens per second of robot motion

scenes.caption: One 7-DoF arm. Per-step binning needs 7 tokens per step: 35 tokens per second at 5 Hz, 140 at 20 Hz. Points are measured token counts per 1-second chunk from the FAST paper.
Two arms (14 dims) at 50 Hz: 700 tokens for one second of motion, the FAST paper's shirt-folding number. FAST stays near 30 tokens per arm per second at every frequency (53 for this task).

blocks.md: Two problems follow. **Speed:** as a simple model, assume a 7B decoder takes 25 ms per token. Seven tokens then take 175 ms, capping control at 5.7 Hz; 14 dims cap it at 2.9 Hz, far from 50 Hz. (OpenVLA's measured 6 Hz is in the same range.) **Learning:** the FAST authors show something worse.

blocks.prompt: Sample one smooth trajectory at higher and higher rates and bin it into 256 bins. Then train an autoregressive model on the token sequences. What happens to the information carried by each new token as the rate goes up?
blocks.reveal: It shrinks toward zero. In a toy trajectory (the one in the DCT figure below, binned over [-1, 1]) the average jump between consecutive bins is 29 at 5 Hz, 3.1 at 50 Hz and 0.78 at 200 Hz, where 29% of tokens simply repeat the previous one. Next-token loss is then nearly minimized by copying, and the FAST paper reports exactly that: at high sampling rates the model ends up copying the first action.

blocks.md: FAST (Frequency-space Action Sequence Tokenization) fixes this by tokenizing a whole **action chunk** at once, compressed. Step 1: normalize each dimension with its 1st and 99th percentiles to [-1, 1]. Step 2: apply the **discrete cosine transform** (DCT, the transform inside JPEG) along time for each dimension. Smooth signals put almost all their energy into a few low-frequency coefficients.

blocks.tex: C_k = s_k \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} x_n \cos\!\left(\frac{\pi (2n+1) k}{2N}\right),\quad s_0 = \sqrt{1/N},\; s_{k>0} = \sqrt{2/N}
blocks.caption: Orthonormal DCT-II of a length-N trajectory x. Coefficient k measures how much of a cosine with k half-periods the trajectory contains; total energy is preserved.

blocks.title: Where the energy of a smooth 50-step trajectory goes

scenes.caption: Trajectory: one dimension, 1 s at 50 Hz, x(t) = 0.6 sin(pi t) + 0.3 t - 0.2 in normalized units. 50 samples go in, 50 coefficients come out; these are the first 10.
The first 3 coefficients hold 98.84% of the energy. The other 47 together hold about 1.2%.

blocks.md: Step 3: **scale and round**, $\bar C = \operatorname{round}(\gamma C)$ with $\gamma = 10$ (FAST's default). This is the only lossy step; small coefficients become 0. Our trajectory keeps 7 nonzero integers out of 50, and reconstructing with the inverse DCT gives an RMS error of 0.014 in normalized units. Step 4: flatten the $D \times H$ integer matrix **low frequencies first, interleaving dimensions**, and compress it with **byte-pair encoding** (BPE, vocabulary 1024), which merges runs of zeros and common coefficient patterns into single tokens.

blocks.title: Quantized DCT coefficients for a 2-dim chunk

scenes.caption: Dimension 1 is the trajectory above; dimension 2 is 0.5 cos(pi t) - 0.1. After round(10 C), dim 1 has 7 nonzero values and dim 2 has 2, out of 50 each. Columns past C9 are all zero.
FAST flattens column by column: C0 of every dim, then C1 of every dim, and so on, giving 23, -6, -7, 25, -13, 0, ... The overall shape of the motion is predicted first.
After position 17 of 100 every value is zero. BPE turns this sparse sequence into a few dense tokens; the naive scheme would need 100 tokens for these 2 dims.

blocks.md: FAST spends tokens on information, not on time steps. Across datasets from 5 Hz to 50 Hz it produced roughly 30 tokens per arm per 1-second chunk, so the token count tracks the complexity of the motion rather than the control rate.

Results reported by the FAST authors: an autoregressive pi0 trained with FAST matches the diffusion version of pi0 while training up to 5x faster, and in DROID evaluations it followed language instructions more closely. The cost is inference: about 750 ms per chunk (30 to 60 tokens through the full 2B backbone) versus under 100 ms for diffusion pi0. They also released **FAST+**, a universal BPE vocabulary trained on 1M real robot action trajectories.

blocks.question: Which step of the FAST pipeline loses information?
options: The DCT, because it drops high frequencies
Byte-pair encoding, because it merges tokens
Scaling and rounding the DCT coefficients
Column-first flattening
blocks.explain: The orthonormal DCT is exactly invertible and BPE is lossless. Rounding the scaled coefficients to integers is where small coefficients become zero; the scale gamma trades compression against reconstruction error.

blocks.question: A bimanual robot (14 action dims) runs at 50 Hz. How many tokens does per-step 256-bin tokenization need for a 1-second chunk?
blocks.explain: 14 dims x 50 steps = 700 tokens, matching the FAST paper's shirt-folding row. FAST needed about 53 for the same chunk.

lessons.title: pi0: denoising a whole action chunk with flow matching

blocks.md: Tokens are not the only way out of the VLM. pi0 (Black et al., 2024) keeps actions **continuous** and generates an **action chunk** $A_t = [a_t, \dots, a_{t+H-1}]$ of $H = 50$ future actions per inference, enough for dexterous control at up to 50 Hz. Why not just regress the chunk with mean squared error? Because demonstrations are **multimodal**: at the same state, one demonstrator goes left around an obstacle and another goes right.

blocks.prompt: Half the demonstrations do chunk R = (0.6, 0.8), half do chunk L = (-0.6, -0.8), from the same observation. A network trained with mean squared error to output one chunk will predict what?
blocks.reveal: The mean, (0, 0): a motion no demonstrator ever made, straight into the obstacle. A generative model instead learns the distribution and samples one mode. Diffusion Policy (Chi et al., 2023) made this argument for robot policies, and pi0 uses flow matching for the same reason.

blocks.md: Architecture: pi0 is one transformer with **two sets of weights**. Images and the language prompt go through a VLM backbone initialized from **PaliGemma** (3B). The robot state $q_t$ (joint angles) and the noisy action tokens go through a smaller **action expert** (about 300M parameters, width 1024) initialized from scratch, for 3.3B in total. The two experts interact only through self-attention.

blocks.title: pi0 inference: cache the prefix, run the expert 10 times

scenes.caption: Images and prompt run once through the VLM. Their attention block cannot see the later blocks, so their keys and values can be cached. 14 ms image encoders plus 32 ms prefix pass on an RTX 4090.
Start from Gaussian noise for the whole 50-step chunk at tau = 0. The action expert reads the noisy chunk and the state, attends to the cached prefix, and outputs a velocity for every action.
An Euler step moves the chunk along the velocity and tau grows by 0.1. Only the small expert reruns: 10 passes take 27 ms in total.
At tau = 1 the chunk is the predicted 50 actions. Total on-board inference: 73 ms for up to 1 s of motion at 50 Hz.

blocks.md: pi0's attention mask has three blocks: [images, language], [state], [noisy actions]. Attention is bidirectional within a block and cannot look at later blocks. The first block cannot see the new robot inputs, which keeps it close to PaliGemma's pretraining; the state block is fixed across denoising steps, so its keys and values are cached too.

blocks.tex: A^\tau = \tau A + (1-\tau)\epsilon,\quad \epsilon \sim \mathcal N(0, I),\qquad \mathcal L = \big\| v_\theta(A^\tau, o) - (A - \epsilon) \big\|^2
blocks.caption: Training (pi0's convention: tau = 0 is pure noise, tau = 1 is data). The target velocity A minus epsilon points from the noise sample straight to the clean chunk. pi0 samples tau from a beta distribution that favors noisier tau.
Inference: forward Euler from noise at tau = 0 to an action chunk at tau = 1.

blocks.md: Toy: a chunk of $H = 2$ one-dimensional actions and two equally likely demonstrated chunks, $R = (0.6, 0.8)$ and $L = (-0.6, -0.8)$. Instead of a trained network we use the exact velocity field for this data, the field a perfectly trained $v_\theta$ would output. It averages each mode's direction, weighted by how likely that mode is to have produced the current noisy chunk:

blocks.tex: v(x, \tau) = \sum_{i \in \{R, L\}} w_i \frac{A_i - x}{1-\tau},\qquad w_i \propto \exp\!\left(-\frac{\|x - \tau A_i\|^2}{2(1-\tau)^2}\right)

blocks.title: Ten Euler steps turn noise into one mode

scenes.caption: tau = 0: the noise sample is (0.25, 0.10). Both modes are equally plausible, so v = mean of modes minus x, pointing toward (0, 0).
tau = 0.2 after two steps: the chunk drifts slightly toward 0, but R is already a bit more likely because the sample started on R's side.
tau = 0.4: R's weight rises to 0.589 and the second action's velocity turns positive.
tau = 0.6: the decision is being made. R's weight is 0.811 and both velocities now point toward R.
tau = 0.7: committed. R's weight is 0.991, and the 1/(1 - tau) factor makes the velocity large so the remaining steps can cover the distance.
tau = 0.8 and 0.9: with all weight on R, the path is a straight line to R at constant velocity (1.303, 1.971).

tau = 1: the chunk is exactly R = (0.6, 0.8). Both actions in the chunk come from the same mode. Simplified: a real network only approximates this field, so the final chunk lands near, not exactly on, a demonstrated chunk.

blocks.md: Other noise samples choose differently: starting from (-0.3, 0.2) the same 10 steps end at L, and from (0.05, -0.02) they end at R. The randomness lives in the initial noise; the integration then commits to one consistent chunk, the property Diffusion Policy calls **temporal action consistency**.
pi0 replaces "decode 7 tokens per step" with "run a 300M expert 10 times per chunk". Cost no longer grows with the number of action dimensions or the control rate, and the output is continuous.

blocks.question: In the toy, you replace the 10 Euler steps with a single step of size 1 from tau = 0. What chunk comes out of the noise sample (0.25, 0.10)?
options: (0.6, 0.8), the R mode
(-0.6, -0.8), the L mode
(0.25, 0.10), unchanged
(0, 0), the average of the modes
blocks.explain: At tau = 0 both weights are 0.5, so v = (mean of modes) - x and x + v is the mean, (0, 0). One big step reproduces the regression failure; several small steps let the weights sharpen before the chunk moves far.

blocks.question: Why does pi0 prevent the image and language tokens from attending to the state and noisy-action tokens?
options: So the prefix's keys and values stay valid across all 10 denoising steps and the prefix stays close to the VLM's pretraining
Because PaliGemma cannot process more than 256 tokens
To make the action expert bidirectional
Because flow matching requires a causal mask over time steps
blocks.explain: If the prefix could see the noisy actions, its keys and values would change every step and could not be cached. The paper also states the mask minimizes distribution shift from PaliGemma's pretraining.

lessons.title: Running action chunks in the control loop

blocks.md: Predicting chunks is older than VLAs. **ACT** (Action Chunking with Transformers, Zhao et al., 2023) predicts the next $k$ actions from each observation instead of one. Every $k$ steps the policy observes, predicts $k$ actions and executes them, a $k$-fold reduction in the task's effective horizon. That mitigates **compounding errors**, where small mistakes push the robot into states the demonstrations never covered.

In ACT's ablation, success rose from 1% at $k = 1$ to 44% at $k = 100$, then tapered at larger $k$ (close to open-loop). Diffusion Policy names the knobs: observe $T_o$ steps, predict $T_p$ steps, execute $T_a$ steps before replanning. Its authors found $T_a = 8$ best for most tasks: longer gives consistent actions, but too long reacts slowly to surprises.

blocks.title: One second of control: per-step tokens vs a pi0 chunk

scenes.caption: OpenVLA: one inference (7 decoded tokens) per action, about 6 Hz on an RTX 4090. Six actions in the first second.
pi0 on a 50 Hz robot: a 73 ms inference yields 50 actions; 25 are executed (0.5 s), then it replans. Simplified: drawn as infer-then-execute; the paper does not detail any overlap.

Side by side: about 6 actions in the first second versus about 43 here (the robot's rate is 50 Hz), because one 73 ms inference (prefix plus 10 expert passes) yields 50 actions instead of one decode yielding one.

blocks.md: Executing a chunk open-loop means new observations arrive abruptly every $k$ steps, which can cause jerky motion. ACT's fix is **temporal ensembling**: query the policy at every step, so several overlapping chunks each hold a prediction for the current step, and average them with exponential weights.

blocks.tex: a_t = \frac{\sum_i w_i A_t[i]}{\sum_i w_i},\qquad w_i = \exp(-m\, i)
blocks.caption: A_t[i] is the i-th prediction for step t, with i = 0 the oldest. A smaller m means new observations are incorporated faster.

blocks.title: Temporal ensembling of 4 predictions for one step

scenes.caption: Four overlapping chunks each predicted the gripper's x position for this step (illustrative values, in meters): 0.40, 0.44, 0.47, 0.52.
Normalized weights with m = 0.5 (illustrative): 0.455, 0.276, 0.167, 0.102. The oldest prediction counts most, so the executed value, 0.435, moves smoothly.

blocks.md: Temporal ensembling is not a universal upgrade. The pi0 authors tried it early and found it hurt performance, so pi0 executes chunks open-loop: 16 actions then replan on 20 Hz robots (every 0.8 s), 25 actions on 50 Hz robots (every 0.5 s).

Putting the three action heads side by side:

- **Per-step binning** (RT-2, OpenVLA): simplest, reuses the LM head unchanged, easy LoRA fine-tuning. Token count grows with dimensions and frequency, so it fits low-rate control.
- **FAST tokens** (pi0-FAST): still plain next-token prediction, about 30 tokens per arm-second, faster training and strong language following. Autoregressive decoding of a chunk is slow (about 750 ms).
- **Flow-matching expert** (pi0): continuous chunks at up to 50 Hz in 73 ms, handles multimodal demonstrations. Needs a separate expert and a denoising loop.

blocks.question: In ACT's temporal ensemble, you lower m from 0.5 to 0.01. What changes?
options: Only the oldest prediction is used
Weights become nearly equal, so newer predictions count about as much as old ones and new observations are incorporated faster
The ensemble becomes a median instead of a mean
The policy is queried less often
blocks.explain: With m near 0, exp(-m i) is close to 1 for every i, so all predictions are averaged almost equally. The ACT paper states that a smaller m means faster incorporation of new observations.

blocks.question: You must control a 14-dim bimanual robot at 50 Hz for laundry folding, where demonstrators fold in different orders. Which action head fits best?
options: Per-step 256-bin tokens, since it needs no extra modules
Mean-squared-error regression of one action per step
A flow-matching action expert that outputs 50-step chunks
Per-step tokens with a larger vocabulary
blocks.explain: Per-step tokens would need 700 tokens per second; regression averages different folding strategies. A flow-matching expert produces continuous 50-step chunks in one short loop and samples one mode, which is what pi0 was built for.

blocks.question: A Diffusion Policy user raises the execution horizon from 8 to 64 steps on a task where objects get bumped. Success drops. Why?
options: Longer chunks are less smooth
The diffusion model cannot predict more than 16 steps
Longer execution horizons increase the number of denoising steps per action
The robot executes many actions without looking, so it reacts slowly when the scene changes
blocks.explain: Executing more steps open-loop improves consistency but delays the next observation. Diffusion Policy's ablation found too long a horizon hurts because of slow reaction time, with 8 steps best for most tasks.
